The sharp drop is a mathematical consequence of the **10-minute SLA target** combined with the **distribution of delivery times**.

**What the playbook says**  
> "The share of orders delivered inside 10 minutes falls off a cliff, not a slope. When average delivery time drifts from roughly 8 minutes to 12 minutes, the share of orders inside 10 minutes can fall from around 90% to under 50%."  
> — *DD-DIAG-001#1*

**Why it happens**  
- The SLA is a **hard threshold**: an order is either delivered ≤ 10 minutes (pass) or > 10 minutes (fail).  
- When the average is ~8 minutes, most orders naturally finish under 10 minutes, so the pass rate is high (~90%).  
- As the average creeps toward 12 minutes, the **entire distribution shifts right**. A much larger fraction of orders now land just past the 10-minute line, so the pass rate collapses (~50% or lower).  
- Small increases in average time therefore produce disproportionately large SLA drops once the average approaches the 10-minute mark.

**Diagnostic reference points** (from *DD-DIAG-001#0*)  
| Stage | Reference target |
|-------|------------------|
| Pick-pack | ~3 minutes |
| Rider wait | ~1.5 minutes |
| Ride (≤ 2 km) | ~5 minutes |
| **Total** | **~9.5 minutes** |

The system is designed around a ~9.5-minute *typical* total. Once the actual average exceeds ~10 minutes, you are already past the SLA line for a large share of orders.

**Practical takeaway**  
Don’t rely on the SLA percentage alone to diagnose *why* it fell. Compare the three stage times (pick-pack, rider wait, ride) against a normal period to see which stage slipped.
